title: Suffering close
hookLine: weeks on a hard question, and no bow tied on it
last: MEN ARE DISTURBED NOT BY THE THINGS WHICH HAPPEN.

cards: If you kept a notebook through this block, it holds an odd collection by now. A pain named plainly. A complaint written the way the psalmists wrote theirs.
The name of a far-off place. A map of what actually helps. A letter to the person you used to be.
A note sent to someone hurting. None of it adds up to a solution, and that's not a failure. The honest ending to weeks on a hard question isn't a bow tied on top.
It's a way of holding what's still there.

teach.h: THE NAMING: THE PAIN AND THE ARROW.
teach.b: First, the naming. The block began with the Buddha, who names suffering before anything else, the way a doctor names an illness, and with the second arrow, the pain we add to the pain.
You can't hold what you won't look at.

teach.h: THE ARGUING: JOB AND THE PSALMS.
teach.b: Second, the arguing. Job sat in the ashes, and his friends "sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."
Then they started explaining, and got it wrong. The Psalms let a person argue with God: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?" Third, the holding.
Sabr in the Quran, Krishna's counsel in the Gita to bear heat and cold, Guru Arjan finding God's will sweet, the Sikh hukam.
Each, in its own words, teaches a way to stay steady inside what can't be changed. Fourth, the company. Shiva, the Jewish house of mourning, with visitors sitting beside the mourners.
Less advice, more presence. A hand on the heart and the plain words: others feel this too. Help from a professional, counted as strength.
Together it doesn't make a theory. It makes a manner. Not forcing a lesson out of pain.
Not hurrying anyone, including yourself. Not ranking whose suffering counts.
The word for that manner is the one this block ends on: gently. Tomorrow the year turns to a question right next to this one, and the same manner will be needed there too.

how: Some people who study suffering across traditions end not with a single answer but with a way of holding pain: slowly, without forcing a lesson, and in company.

o: the man who lost nearly everything and sat in the ashes
a friend who said suffering was always punishment
a prophet who wrote the book of Psalms in exile

games.q: the block's four movements — tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha and the second arrow

it ended with several answers kept apart, and a manner: gently.
Job's friends sat silent with him seven days before they spoke
Job 2:13. the trouble began when they started explaining.
the Psalms never complain to God
Psalm 13 asks, how long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?

games.q: the block on suffering is over. what does this block hand you to carry?
o: one final answer to why we suffer.
a manner of holding pain: gently.
the rule that pain always teaches a lesson.
games.why: no single answer, and no forced lesson. the block ends on a manner: name it, argue if you must, hold steady, keep company, gently.

practice: Sit gently; that's the whole practice. Let the body be heavy and the breath come at its own pace, and if something hard from these weeks comes back, let it sit beside you, the way Job's friends sat before they spoke.
If your mind wanders, bring it back the way you'd guide a child by the hand, not the way you'd yank a leash.

wordCard.voice: Job, who sat in the ashes while his friends kept silent before they started explaining, and got it wrong. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: gently. Nothing in these weeks has to be solved first. See you tomorrow.
